title: LLM-JEPA: Large Language Models Meet Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures
description: There is a long-standing divide at the heart of representation learning. On one side you have generative methods, which learn by reconstructing their inputs — predicting the next token, filling in masked patches, or decoding a compressed representation back to pixel space. On the other side you have Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures, or JEPAs, which instead operate entirely in embedding space: they learn by predicting the embedding of one view of an input from the embedding of another view, with no attempt to reconstruct the original. In vision, this distinction has turned out to matter enormously. JEPA-style objectives consistently outperform reconstruction objectives on perception and knowledge-discovery tasks, partly because they escape the biases introduced by operating in raw input space — the kind of fine-grained pixel-level detail that is irrelevant to understanding a scene.

title: Green Shielding: A Framework for User-Level Query Variation in Medical AI
description: The central problem this paper addresses is deceptively simple: large language models behave differently depending on how you ask them things. Not adversarially — not jailbreaks or prompt injections — but in the ordinary, routine ways that real users happen to phrase their questions. A patient who writes a worried, first-person message gets a different medical response than one who writes a calm, third-person clinical description of the same condition. The authors call their framework for studying this Green Shielding, and they instantiate it in the domain of medical diagnosis.

title: Predicting the impact of treatments over time with uncertainty aware neural differential equations
description: Predicting the impact of treatments from observational data is a major unsolved challenge despite significant recent advances in time series modeling. When clinicians decide who receives a treatment, their decisions are typically correlated with the very features that predict outcomes — a patient's blood pressure, disease trajectory, overall prognosis. This confounding means that the population of treated patients looks systematically different from the untreated population, creating a distribution shift between what we observe and what we want to predict. Prior work on addressing this usually assumes a positive level of statistical overlap between treated and untreated groups, but overlap is both difficult to verify and rarely satisfied in practice.

title: Quick Take — Predicting the impact of treatments over time with uncertainty aware neural differential equations
description: The core problem in treatment effect estimation from observational data is confounding: patients who receive a treatment tend to be systematically different from those who don't, so comparing outcomes directly gives biased estimates. Most methods that try to correct for this require an assumption called positive overlap — that for any patient history, both treated and untreated outcomes are actually observed somewhere in the data. In practice this assumption is hard to verify and frequently violated. This paper takes a different angle: rather than trying harder to satisfy the overlap assumption, accept that it may fail and build a model that knows when it doesn't know.

title: Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
description: Synthetic data generation has become a cornerstone of modern data science, promising a way to address both data scarcity and privacy concerns simultaneously. This paper asks a precise question: can high-fidelity synthetic data actually make statistical methods more accurate — and if so, how much synthetic data should you use?

title: Quick Take — Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
description: The central question this paper addresses is whether high-fidelity synthetic data — generated by modern generative models like diffusion models — can actually improve statistical methods that were designed to run on real data. This sounds almost paradoxical: why would training on fake data help? The field has had mixed evidence on this, and this paper proposes a unified framework to understand when and how it works.

title: Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
description: Synthetic data generation, a cornerstone of generative artificial intelligence, promises to reshape data science by addressing two persistent challenges: data scarcity and privacy. As synthetic data becomes more prevalent, a natural question arises — are the statistical methods we apply to it actually reliable? This paper investigates both sides of that question. On the effectiveness side, the authors introduce the Synthetic Data Generation for Analytics framework, which they call Syn. The framework applies statistical methods to high-fidelity synthetic data produced by generative models that have been fine-tuned on raw data using transfer learning. A central finding is the generational effect: as more synthetic data is added, accuracy tends to improve and then plateau or even worsen, pointing to the existence of a reflection point — an ideal synthetic sample size beyond which generation errors begin to dominate. Three case studies validate the framework across sentiment analysis, predictive modeling of structured data, and statistical inference on tabular data. On the privacy side, synthetic data imposes lower risk than raw data while remaining compatible with the differential privacy standard.

title: Quick Take — Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
description: The question this paper addresses is whether high-fidelity synthetic data can systematically improve the accuracy of standard statistical methods — not just as a privacy tool or a data-sharing mechanism, but as a direct performance booster. This is genuinely contested territory: some prior work finds synthetic data helps, other work finds it hurts, and the field has lacked a principled framework for understanding when and why either outcome occurs.

title: Quick Take — Statistical ranking with dynamic covariates
description: The Plackett-Luce model and its pairwise special case, the Bradley-Terry model, are workhorses for learning latent scores from comparison data — sports rankings, RLHF preference learning, any setting where you observe which item in a group wins. A natural extension is to let covariates shift those scores: a tennis player is older now, a product is shown in a different context. Prior work either drops individual effects entirely and models scores as pure functions of covariates, or keeps individual effects but fixes the covariates so they don't vary across comparisons. Neither is fully satisfying. This paper fills that gap.

title: Statistical ranking with dynamic covariates
description: Statistical ranking models built on the Plackett–Luce framework assign each object a latent score, and the probability of any observed ranking is determined by those scores. Most prior work assumes that each object's score is fixed — the same no matter which comparison it appears in. This paper introduces a generalization where covariates attached to each object can vary across comparisons, meaning the same player or horse may carry a different covariate value in every race or match. The authors call this the PlusDC model — Plackett–Luce Supplemented with Dynamic Covariates. The paper provides conditions for when the model is identifiable, when the maximum likelihood estimator uniquely exists, an efficient algorithm to compute it, and a uniform consistency theorem with explicit convergence rates. Both synthetic experiments and applications to ATP tennis and Hong Kong horse racing show the model improving over the standard Plackett–Luce baseline.

title: Full Read — Statistical ranking with dynamic covariates
description: We introduce a general covariate-assisted statistical ranking model within the Plackett–Luce framework. Unlike previous studies focusing on individual effects with fixed covariates, our model allows covariates to vary across comparisons. This added flexibility enhances model fitting yet brings significant challenges in analysis. This paper addresses these challenges in the context of maximum likelihood estimation. We first provide sufficient and necessary conditions for both model identifiability and the unique existence of the maximum likelihood estimator. Then, we develop an efficient alternating maximization algorithm to compute the maximum likelihood estimator. Under suitable assumptions on the design of comparison graphs and covariates, we establish a uniform consistency result for the maximum likelihood estimator, with convergence rates determined by the asymptotic graph connectivity. We also construct random designs where the proposed assumptions hold almost surely. Numerical studies are conducted to support our findings and demonstrate the model's application to real-world datasets, including horse racing and tennis competitions.

title: Quick Take — The frontier of simulation-based inference
description: Many branches of science rely on complex simulators to model phenomena they care about — particle collisions, epidemic spread, neuron dynamics, cosmological structure formation. These simulators are often excellent forward models, but they create a fundamental problem for inference: the likelihood function is intractable. You can run the simulator and get data out, but you cannot evaluate the probability of a particular observation under a given set of parameters. This paper is a review of the rapidly evolving field that has grown up around this problem, written by three researchers who have been central contributors to it.

title: The frontier of simulation-based inference
description: Many domains of science have developed complex simulations to describe phenomena of interest. While these simulations provide high-fidelity models, they are poorly suited for inference and lead to challenging inverse problems. This paper reviews the rapidly developing field of simulation-based inference and identifies the forces giving new momentum to the field. It describes how the frontier is expanding so that a broad audience can appreciate the profound change these developments may have on science.

title: Full Read — The frontier of simulation-based inference
description: Many domains of science have developed complex simulations to describe phenomena of interest. While these simulations provide high-fidelity models, they are poorly suited for inference and lead to challenging inverse problems. We review the rapidly developing field of simulation-based inference and identify the forces giving new momentum to the field. Finally, we describe how the frontier is expanding so that a broad audience can appreciate the profound change these developments may have on science.

title: Quick Take — Martingale posterior distributions
description: Traditional Bayesian inference starts by placing a prior distribution over a parameter and then updates it to a posterior after observing data. This paper argues that framing is backwards, or at least incomplete. The real source of uncertainty is not ignorance about a parameter in the abstract — it is the simple fact that you have not seen the entire population. If you had all the data, the parameter would be known exactly. This reframing, grounded in a classical result from Doob, has been sitting in the foundations of probability theory since 1949. This paper finally builds a full inference framework on top of it.

title: Martingale posterior distributions
description: The prior distribution on the parameters of a sampling model is the usual starting point for Bayesian uncertainty quantification. This paper offers a different perspective. The authors argue that statistical uncertainty exists not because parameters are inherently random, but because we have not observed the entire population. If we had, the quantity of interest would be known precisely. Bayesian inference, viewed this way, is fundamentally about constructing a distribution on the missing observations, conditional on what has been seen. In the conditionally independent and identically distributed setting with an observed sample of size n, the Bayesian therefore assigns a predictive distribution on all the future data that haven't been collected yet, which in turn induces a distribution on any statistic of interest.
